profile.reading:
This Lumen colocation facility is located at 300 West Lexington Street, Baltimore, MD 21201, per public property records; Lumen does not publish individual building addresses or specs on its own site for any of its 175-plus North American colocation sites. Lumen Technologies, formerly CenturyLink (renamed Lumen on September 14, 2020, with its stock ticker changing from CTL to LUMN on September 18, 2020) and built in part on CenturyLink's November 1, 2017 acquisition of Level 3 Communications, operates this facility as part of a network-centric edge colocation product rather than a wholesale hyperscale campus. Lumen's own colocation data sheet states more than 175 carrier-neutral data centers across more than 60 North American markets, offering cabinet power in the 3 to 15 kilowatt range described as varying by site; unlike the wholesale operators tracked elsewhere in this registry, Lumen does not disclose per-building square footage or total MW capacity for any of its sites.

Data center growth is straining the mid-Atlantic PJM grid that serves Baltimore. Data centers' share of PJM-wide load is projected to triple between 2024 and 2029; PJM capacity auction costs jumped from about $2 billion to nearly $15 billion in the 2024-25 auction and just over $16 billion in the 2026-27 auction. Maryland has retired 6,000 megawatts of generation since 2018 while adding only 1,600 megawatts, leaving the state importing roughly 40% of its electricity; two Talen Energy plants near Baltimore had their planned retirement pushed from May 2025 to 2029, at an estimated $629 million cost to consumers, per the Maryland Office of People's Counsel. Baltimore Gas and Electric separately requested an $8-per-month, $156 million electric rate increase in July 2026 under Maryland's Utility RELIEF Act, a request state ratepayer advocates plan to challenge before the Public Service Commission.

reading.body:
Lumen Baltimore is a colocation facility in downtown Baltimore whose power capacity is not published. The operator, Lumen Technologies, acquired it as part of its legacy telecom infrastructure or through the Level 3 merger in 2017, though the company divested most of its dedicated data center business to Cyxtera in that year and specific ownership records for individual buildings are not public. Without a published power figure, the facility's relevance to AI infrastructure cannot be assessed from available data.

Maryland has 11 mapped data center facilities and only 3 with published power capacity totaling 9.3 MW. Lumen Baltimore ranks fourth by published capacity in the state, meaning at least three other Maryland facilities have disclosed their power draw while this one has not. The state's total published capacity is modest by national standards for AI infrastructure buildout.

The facility's role in supporting AI workloads depends entirely on specifications Lumen has not made public. No dedicated product page, market description, or capacity statement for this location appears in the operator's current web presence, leaving its technical specifications, power delivery, cooling, and network connectivity unknown to prospective users or researchers tracking AI infrastructure.
